newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England: Key dates spanning three centuries.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England: Key dates spanning three centuries.

text.p: The Bank of England's relationship with the British government returned to the spotlight on Tuesday, after the new ruling Labour government set a series of reforms to grant the central bank more independence.
Known as "The Old Lady," the central bank has been around for more than 300 years. Here are some key events in its colourful history, mainly based on information from the Bank of England.

July 1694 - The Bank of England is founded to raise 1.2 million pounds ($2 million) for the government of William and Mary to fight the wars against France. The Bank of England is granted a royal charter and is the only joint stock bank allowed.
It opens with a staff of 17 clerks and two doorkeepers.
1715 - From 1715 onwards, the Bank regularly raised money for the government by selling government bonds.
1734 - The Bank moves into its present day premises at Threadneedle Street in the heart of London's financial district and gradually expands to fill the three-acre site.
1780 - The Bank is threatened by a mob during the Gordon Riots and the government agrees to provide an overnight military guard. This was only discontinued in 1973.
1797 - The Napoleonic wars strain the government's finances and drains the Bank's gold reserves, making it necessary to stop paying out gold in exchange for the Bank's notes.

1821 - This restriction period ends and financial discipline is restored. During the period, the Bank issued one and two pound notes for the first time, extremely tempting to counterfeiters, 300 of whom were hanged during the period.
1826 - The Banking Act allows joint stock banks other than the Bank of England, leading to a big increase in banks.
1827 - The Bank opens its provincial branches.

1844 - The Bank Charter Act gives the Bank a formal monopoly of issuing notes in England and Wales. Scottish banks, which continued to issue their own notes, are required to back these with holdings of Bank of England notes.
The Bank begins its present day practice of publishing a separate balance sheet for its note issuing activities, the profits of which are paid direct to the British Treasury.

1890 - Baring Brothers hits trouble after unwise loans in South America and the Bank of England rescues the bank, using a fund to which it and other banks subscribed, establishing the concept of lender of last resort.

The Bank began to routinely use this leverage over the banking system's liquidity to set interest rates. While the gold standard was in place, the choice of interest rate was constrained but later, it became more a matter of discretion.
1914-1918 - The link with gold is broken again.
1925 - The Bank tries to return to the gold standard.
1931 - The gold standard is finally abandoned. Gold and foreign exchange reserves are transferred to the Treasury but still managed by the Bank, and the note issue becomes entirely fiduciary.

1946 - The Bank of England is nationalised, transferring ownership to the government from private stockholders. The Nationalisation Act also gives the government the power to issue "directions" to the Bank.
1979 -The Banking Act confirms the Bank's powers in law, and gives it a formal statutory responsibility for the supervision of banks.
September 1984 - The Bank rescued Johnson Matthey Bank, buying it for one pound and putting in its own managers to run it.

1991 - The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) collapses and is closed with debts of more than $12 billion amid evidence of massive fraud and money laundering. A parliamentary investigation into the collapse later was critical of the Bank's handling of the affair.
February 1995 - Barings collapses under the weight of $1.4 bln of losses on unauthorised derivatives trades in Singapore. Another investigation into the Bank's actions was launched.
May 2, 1997 - New Labour government begins following May 1 election in first Labour administration for 18 years.

May 6, 1997 - New Chancellor Brown forms monetary policy committee to set interest rates (government has no voting rights on committee). Brown gives Bank responsibility for achieving inflation aims as set by the Treasury.

Background - The Bank is headed by Governor Eddie George, the seventh governor since nationalisation and the 118th since it was founded. With staff of around 4,500, it issues some 1.4 billion new notes a year, destroying a similar number of used notes.
